title: React core: rendering, state, effects, keys (variant 1)
description: Predict what a component shows and when it renders; pick the fix a senior would pick.

domains.name: State as a snapshot, updates, immutability
Effects: dependencies, cleanup, when not to use one

questions.stem: No React Compiler. `App` holds a `count` state and renders `<Header />`, which takes no props and is not wrapped in `memo`. You click the button that calls `setCount(c => c + 1)`. What happens to `Header`?

options.text: It renders again, because a parent's render renders its children by default
options.why: React re-runs every child of a component that rendered, unless the child bails out (memo with equal props).

options.text: It is skipped, because React notices it received no props at all
options.why: Tempting, but 'no props' isn't checked. Only `memo` compares props; without it the child renders with the parent.

options.text: It is unmounted and mounted again with fresh state on every parent update
options.why: Re-rendering is not remounting. Its state survives, because the same component type sits at the same position.

options.text: It renders only if the browser DOM of Header would actually change after the click
options.why: The DOM diff happens after rendering. React renders first, then commits only the DOM differences.

questions.explain: Rendering means React calls your component function. When a component renders, its children render too, by default. That is usually cheap; the DOM is only touched where the output changed. `memo` (or the React Compiler) is how a child opts out.

questions.stem: No React Compiler. `const Row = memo(function Row({ onSelect }) {...})`. The parent renders `<Row onSelect={() => select(id)} />` and re-renders every time a search box above it changes. A profiler shows `Row` still renders on every keystroke. Why?

options.text: `memo` only works on components that have no props at all
options.why: memo compares props shallowly; it is meant for components with props.

options.text: The arrow function is a new object every render, so the shallow prop comparison fails
options.why: `Object.is(oldFn, newFn)` is false for a freshly created function, so memo has to render. Wrap it in useCallback or pass `id` and a stable handler.

options.text: Profiling builds disable memo, so the profiler is not showing the production behaviour you would see
options.why: memo works in profiling builds; the renders are real.

options.text: Search input state changes always force every component on the page to render
options.why: Only the component that owns the state and its subtree render, and memo can cut that subtree.

questions.explain: memo skips a render only when every prop is `Object.is`-equal to last time. Inline functions, objects and arrays are new each render, so they defeat memo. Stabilise them (useCallback/useMemo), or let the React Compiler do it.

questions.stem: Inside `function Form() { ... }` a teammate declared `function Field() { const [v, setV] = useState(''); return <input value={v} onChange={e => setV(e.target.value)} /> }` and renders `<Field />`. `Form` re-renders on every keystroke. Users report the input loses focus and clears after each letter. What is the cause?

options.text: The input is controlled, and controlled inputs always lose focus while state updates
options.why: Controlled inputs keep focus normally; millions of forms rely on that.

options.text: `useState('')` resets itself whenever the value it was given changes
options.why: The initial value is used only on the first render of that component instance.

options.text: `Field` is a new component type on each `Form` render, so React unmounts the old one and mounts a new one
options.why: React compares element types by identity. A function declared inside a render is a different function each time, so its state and DOM are thrown away.

options.text: The event handler should call `e.preventDefault()` to stop the browser from resetting the field
options.why: Nothing in the browser resets it; React replaces the DOM node because the type changed.

questions.explain: Never define components inside other components. Move `Field` to the top level (pass what it needs as props). Same type at the same position = state kept; a different type = state reset.

questions.stem: In development, a `console.log('render')` at the top of a component body prints twice per render. In the production build it prints once. The app is wrapped in `<StrictMode>`. What is going on?

options.text: Strict Mode calls component functions twice in development to expose impure rendering
options.why: A pure component gives the same result both times; a side effect in render shows up as a duplicate.

options.text: There is a bug: something triggers a second state update right after the first render completes
options.why: Then production would show it too. The difference between dev and prod points at Strict Mode.

options.text: The dev server's hot reload mounts every component twice
options.why: Hot reload re-runs changed modules; it doesn't double every render.

options.text: React renders once for the virtual DOM and once more for the real DOM
options.why: There is one render, then a commit; React doesn't call your function per tree.

questions.explain: Strict Mode (development only) double-invokes component bodies, initialisers and reducers, and runs effect setup → cleanup → setup once on mount. It is a test for purity and missing cleanups, not a bug to work around.

questions.stem: `count` starts at 0. A click handler runs:

options.text: 3, because each call adds one to the latest value
options.why: Each call reads `count` from this render's snapshot, which is 0 every time.

options.text: 1, because all three calls compute 0 + 1 from the same snapshot
options.why: They queue 'set to 1' three times. Use `setCount(c => c + 1)` to build on the queued value.

options.text: It throws a warning because state is set several times in one handler
options.why: Setting state several times in one handler is allowed and batched.

options.text: 3, but the screen updates three separate times one after another so you see it count up
options.why: React batches the updates into one render, and the result is 1 anyway.

questions.explain: State is a snapshot: within one render, `count` never changes. Updates are batched and applied for the next render. When the next value depends on the previous one, pass an updater function.

questions.stem: A handler does `setStep(5); console.log(step);` while `step` is 2. A teammate says the log proves `setStep` is broken. What does the log print, and why?

options.text: 5, because setState is synchronous inside event handlers but async elsewhere
options.why: An old explanation; `step` is a constant of this render either way.

options.text: 2, because `step` is this render's value; the new value arrives in the next render
options.why: `step` is a plain const captured by the handler. Calling the setter asks for a new render; it doesn't change the variable.

options.text: undefined, because state is cleared while the update is waiting in React's queue
options.why: State is never cleared between renders.

options.text: 2 the first time and 5 if you click it again quickly enough before the next render
options.why: The second click runs a handler from a newer render; it would print 5 there because that render's snapshot is 5, not because of timing.

questions.explain: Read the new value where it exists: in the next render (or compute it in the handler: `const next = 5; setStep(next); use(next)`). Logging right after the setter always shows the old snapshot.

questions.stem: A todo list adds items with `todos.push(newTodo); setTodos(todos);`. Clicking 'Add' does nothing on screen, but the array in the console has the new item. Which fix is right?

options.text: Call `forceUpdate()` after `setTodos` so the list refreshes
options.why: Function components have no forceUpdate, and forcing hides the real bug: mutation.

options.text: `setTodos([...todos, newTodo])`, so React receives a new array
options.why: React compares with `Object.is`; the same mutated array looks unchanged, so the update is skipped.

options.text: Move `todos` into a `useRef`, because refs are designed for values that change often
options.why: Changing a ref never re-renders; the list would still not update.

options.text: Wrap the push in `useEffect` so it runs after render
options.why: Still a mutation of the same array; still no change React can see.

questions.explain: Treat state as read-only. Create a new array or object (`[...a, x]`, `a.filter`, `a.map`, `{...o, k: v}`, `toSorted`) and pass that to the setter. Mutation breaks both re-rendering and memo.

questions.stem: A form keeps `firstName` and `lastName` in state, plus `fullName` in a third state that a `useEffect` sets whenever either name changes. The UI briefly shows the old full name after typing. What would a senior change?

options.text: Compute `fullName` from the two names during render, and delete the third state and its effect
options.why: Derived values belong in render: always in sync, one render instead of two, less code.

options.text: Use `useLayoutEffect` instead, so the full name is updated before the browser paints the stale value
options.why: It hides the flash but keeps the extra render and the duplicated state.

options.text: Add `fullName` to the dependency array
options.why: That adds a loop risk and doesn't remove the stale first render.

options.text: Store all three in one object state
options.why: Still duplicated data that can drift; the derived value is still stored.

questions.explain: If you can calculate something from props or state, don't store it. Calculate it while rendering (with `useMemo` only if it's measurably expensive). Effects that only set state from other state are the most common 'you might not need an effect' case.

questions.stem: A component fetches products and the tab freezes with thousands of network requests:

options.text: `fetch` must be awaited inside the effect
options.why: Promise chains are fine; the problem is when the effect runs.

options.text: There is no dependency array, so the effect runs after every render, and each fetch sets state, which renders again
options.why: No array = run after every render. `setItems(data)` always sets a new array, so it loops forever.

options.text: The server returns a new array every time, which React rejects
options.why: React accepts any value; the new array is what keeps triggering renders.

options.text: Effects cannot call setState
options.why: They can; it just has to be guarded by the right dependencies.

questions.explain: Dependencies decide when an effect re-runs: none = every render, `[]` = after mount only, `[a, b]` = when a or b change. For data fetching in real apps, a library (TanStack Query, SWR) or your framework's loader also handles caching and races.

questions.stem: A profile page fetches `/api/users/${userId}` in an effect with `[userId]`. Clicking quickly from user 1 to user 2 sometimes shows user 1's data under user 2's name. What fixes it properly?

options.text: Debounce the clicks by 300 ms
options.why: Narrows the window but a slow response can still arrive last.

options.text: Return a cleanup that ignores or aborts the old request (an `ignore` flag or `AbortController`)
options.why: The cleanup runs before the next effect, so a late response from the old userId is dropped.

options.text: Move the fetch into the render body so it happens synchronously
options.why: Fetching in render fires on every render and still can't be awaited.

options.text: Add `user` to the dependency array as well as `userId`, so both are tracked together
options.why: More re-runs, same race: responses can still arrive out of order.

questions.explain: Async results can arrive in any order. Every effect that starts async work should clean up: set `ignore = true` (or `controller.abort()`) in the cleanup, and only set state if not ignored.

questions.stem: A timer is supposed to count up every second, but the screen shows 1 and stays at 1:

options.text: `setInterval` doesn't work inside effects; use `setTimeout` recursively
options.why: Intervals work; the callback reads a stale value.

options.text: The interval callback closed over `count` from the first render (0), so it sets 1 forever; use `setCount(c => c + 1)`
options.why: With `[]` the effect runs once, so its closure always sees count = 0. The updater form reads the latest state.

options.text: The cleanup clears the interval right after the first tick
options.why: Cleanup runs on unmount here (deps never change), not after a tick.

options.text: React batches interval updates together and only applies them all when the component unmounts
options.why: Updates from intervals are applied normally, each causing a render.

questions.explain: Closures capture the values of the render they were created in (a 'stale closure'). Either list the value as a dependency (and accept the re-subscribe), or use an updater function so you don't need the value at all.

questions.stem: Product wants an analytics event when the user clicks 'Buy'. A teammate sets `bought` state in the click handler and sends the event in a `useEffect` that watches `bought`. Where should the event be sent?

options.text: Keep the effect, but wrap the send in `if (bought)` so it only fires once the flag has turned true
options.why: Still fires on remounts and Strict Mode re-runs, and still ties a user action to rendering.

options.text: In the click handler itself, because it is caused by that specific interaction
options.why: Code that runs because the user did something belongs in the event handler.

options.text: In a `useLayoutEffect`, so it fires before paint
options.why: Timing isn't the problem; the event isn't caused by rendering.

options.text: In the render body, right after reading `bought`
options.why: Render must be pure; side effects there run on every render.

questions.explain: Ask: why does this code run? Because the component appeared on screen → an effect. Because the user clicked → the event handler. Effects are for synchronising with outside systems, not for reacting to your own events.

questions.stem: A list renders `items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} item={item} />)`. Each `Row` has its own uncontrolled `<input>` for a note. A new item is added to the **top** of the list. Notes now appear next to the wrong items. Why?

options.text: Keys must be strings, and numbers are converted unpredictably
options.why: Numbers are fine as keys; the problem is what the number refers to.

options.text: Index keys follow positions, so every Row keeps its old position's state when the items shift down
options.why: Key 0 was item A and is now the new item, so React reuses A's Row (and its input) for it. Use a stable id: `key={item.id}`.

options.text: Uncontrolled inputs never keep their values when the list they belong to changes size
options.why: They keep them; they just stay with the key, which here points at the wrong item.

options.text: `map` creates new elements, so all inputs reset
options.why: They don't reset; they get matched to the wrong items, which is worse.

questions.explain: A key tells React which item an element is, across renders. Use a stable id from the data. Index keys are only safe when the list never reorders, filters or inserts.

questions.stem: `<EditProfile user={selected} />` keeps form fields in local state initialised from `user`. When you pick another user in the sidebar, the form still shows the previous user's draft. What is the cleanest fix?

options.text: Add a `useEffect` that resets every field when `user` changes
options.why: Works, but renders the stale draft first and must be updated whenever a field is added.

options.text: Render `<EditProfile key={selected.id} user={selected} />` so a new user gets a fresh component
options.why: A different key at the same position means a different component instance, so React resets all its state.

options.text: Use `useMemo` to recompute the initial state values whenever the `user` prop object changes between renders
options.why: useState only reads its initial value once; recomputing it has no effect.

options.text: Move the form state to a global store
options.why: Doesn't decide when to reset; you'd still need to reset per user.

questions.explain: The key isn't only for lists. Changing an element's key tells React 'this is a different thing', which resets its state and its subtree's state in one move.

questions.stem: A glossary renders pairs and React warns 'Each child in a list should have a unique key prop', although each `<dt>` has `key={term.id}`:

options.text: `<dd>` needs a key too, because every element inside a mapped list needs one
options.why: Only the outermost element returned from map needs a key.

options.text: The key belongs on the outermost element: use `<Fragment key={term.id}>` around the pair
options.why: The short `<>` syntax can't take a key; `Fragment` imported from React can.

options.text: Definition lists can't be rendered with `map`
options.why: They can; it's a key placement issue only.

options.text: Combine the keys as `term.id + 'dt'` and `term.id + 'dd'` so every element gets its own unique string
options.why: Uniqueness isn't the problem; the key is on the wrong element.

questions.explain: React reads the key on what `map` returns. When that is a fragment, use `<Fragment key=…>`; the `<></>` shorthand doesn't accept attributes.
